newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish minister threatens to freeze alcohol prices.
newsitem.headline: Irish minister threatens to freeze alcohol prices.

text.p: Drop the price of a pint or a price fixing order will be enforced, Irish minister for commerce, science and technology Pat Rabbitte warned Irish publicans.

Rabbitte on Thursday met representatives of the Licensed Vintners Association (LVA) to discuss recent increases in the price of beer, noting that no price increase was imposed on beer by finance minister Ruairi Quinn in Ireland's annual budget, unveiled on January 22.

In a joint statement, issued after the meeting with the LVA, Rabbitte warned that if publicans who had increased prices did not drop them again he would enforce a price fixing order and freeze prices at their November 1996 level.
A number of Dublin publicans had imposed price increases of up to 5.0 pence a pint over the last two months and this number had risen over the last week, Rabbitte said in the statement.
Concern over recent price rises has prompted Ireland's Competition Authority to announce its intention to review the Irish drinks industry.

"The study will ... focus on barriers to entry and the impact of the licensing laws on the structure of and behaviour in the market," the LVA said, adding that it will decide its own terms of reference at a formal meeting next week.

Minister for Enterprise and Employment Richard Bruton welcomed the Authority's decision. "I believe that we badly need a root and branch review of the whole drinks market from the malting house to the public house," Bruton said in a statement.
"The lack of competition in Ireland is adding 40 Irish pence to the price of the pint of stout," Trinity College economist John Fingleton told Irish national radio, RTE on Friday.
He said the dominance of the beer market by major brewer Guinness and the tight restrictions imposed on the issuing of new licenses were the key factors in pushing the price of the pint so high.
Drinkers at the Dicey Reilly's Pub in the west of Ireland town of Sligo have no such worries as customers can enjoy three pints for a mere 5.0 punts ($8), the Examiner newspaper reported on Friday.
Rural publican Kevin Leydon charges just one penny a pint if his customers get their orders in while a Guinness advertisment is being shown on national television, the Examiner reports.
